 5 lawyers explain a grandson's rights in his grandfather's property while his father is alive
 By Rajeev Kumar 7 min read | Updated on November 16, 2026, 19:06 IST
 Preferred news source Select Upstox as your Preferred news source SUMMARY
 Experts say that the expression ‘ancestral property’ cannot be used as a standalone basis for claiming a share.
 Under Hindu succession law, the manner in which the property devolves is the determining factor. | Representational image/AI generated
 A boy born on January 6, 1994 claimed half of the 1,811 sq ft that came to his father in a family partition a month after his birth. He argued that as a grandson he became a coparcener in his grandfather's property by birth, and that a compromise decree passed after he was born, and without him as a party, could not defeat that right.

 However, the Supreme Court on November 6, 2026 dismissed his appeal, holding that a son's son is not a Class I heir under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act and gets no right by birth in his grandfather's property while his father is alive. 
 A quick reading of the SC judgement indicate that a grandson's claim to a share in his grandfather's property must rest on the property still being undivided joint family property. Once Section 8 succession and a partition intervene, the father's share is his own, and he may sell it.
 While this judgement has been widely reported over the last few days, confusion persists among readers about its exact implications. In this article, five practicing lawyers explain what the SC judgement means for your property rights.
 Alay Razvi, Managing Partner, Accord Juris 
 When a father inherits property individually under Section 8, neither his daughter nor his son acquires a share by birth. He can ordinarily sell, gift or bequeath that property. If he dies without a valid will, his daughter inherits as a Class I heir, with the same entitlement as a son, alongside other eligible heirs.
 The important question is how the father acquired the property, not simply whether it once belonged to the grandfather.
 Tushar Nair, Advocate, Delhi High Court 
 The Supreme Court Bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal have turned down a grandson’s claim to half of a plot that fell to his father on partition of the grandfather’s estate, which was later sold by him. It has been held that what a son inherits under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act is his own, does not continue as a joint family property in which his children acquire a right by birth, and he may sell, gift or will it away without their consent.
 A similar position was also clarified recently by another bench in Darubai v. Kamalabai, though not relied upon, holding that Class-I heirs under Section 8 take as tenants-in-common with defined shares. Read together, the two rulings settle the position on treating such property as joint family property, whether among the heirs or in the next generation.
 The property is only to be treated as ‘ancestral’ because of the way it devolves, not merely because it belonged to a grandfather.
 Sanya Gangar, Associate, PSL Advocates & Solicitors 
 The Supreme Court has held that a son does not acquire a right by birth in property inherited by his father from the grandfather under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, merely by virtue of the property’s ancestral origin.
 Under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a son who inherits his father’s property holds it in his individual capacity, and it does not, by that inheritance alone, become coparcenary property in which his own children acquire an automatic interest.
 The Supreme Court has distinguished devolution by intestate succession under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 from devolution of an interest in coparcenary property under Section 6, and the rights of descendants must be determined on that basis.
 Grahita Agarwal, Senior Associate, B. Shanker Advocates LLP 
 Under Hindu succession law, merely because a property originally belonged to the grandfather, it does not automatically become an ancestral property in the hands of the subsequent generations. The manner in which the property devolves is the determining factor.
 Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act provides for individual succession, and property inherited under this provision is ordinarily treated as the heir's individual property. Therefore, a son cannot assert a birthright merely on the basis of the property's ancestral origin.
 The distinction between an ancestral property and a property inherited through succession is fundamental to Hindu law. Every inheritance from a father or grandfather does not create a coparcenary right in the next generation.
 The Courts examine the nature of devolution and the applicable provisions of succession law before determining whether a child can claim a share by birth. The claim must be supported by the legal character of the property and not merely its family history.
 The judgment reiterates an important principle: the origin of a property and its legal character are two different things. A property inherited by a father under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act does not automatically retain the character of ancestral property in relation to his children. Consequently, children cannot restrain the father from dealing with such property merely by asserting a prospective inheritance.
 These disputes often arise because families tend to use the expression 'ancestral property' loosely.
 However, under Hindu law, the classification has specific legal consequences.
 Whether a property is ancestral, coparcenary or individually inherited must be determined by examining the chain of title and the mode of succession. A claim of birthright cannot succeed merely because the property has remained within the family for generations.
 Kashish Seth, Partner, Trinetra Legal 
 What makes this judgment significant is the distinction it draws between the traditional concept of ancestral property under Mitakshara Hindu law and property devolving by statutory succession under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
 Ordinarily, under Mitakshara law, a son acquires an interest by birth in coparcenary property. However, the mere fact that a property has come from the grandfather does not automatically make it coparcenary property in the hands of the father. The manner in which the father acquired the property becomes decisive.
 The Supreme Court, relying on the settled position in CWT v. Chander Sen, reiterated that where property devolves upon a son under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, he inherits it in his individual capacity and not as the Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family. This distinction is important because the Class I Schedule recognises the son as an heir but does not recognise the son of a living son as an independent heir to the deceased grandfather’s estate.
 In the present case, the grandfather’s estate had already devolved upon his Class I heirs following his death. Thereafter, a compromise decree of partition allotted specific properties to the respective heirs. The father’s share consequently became his exclusive property. The appellant, whose father was alive, could not claim an independent coparcenary interest in that property merely by virtue of his birth.
 The practical takeaway is that the expression ‘ancestral property’ cannot be used as a standalone basis for claiming a share. In a dispute of this nature, the first question must be how the property came into the hands of the present owner: whether it devolved by succession under Section 8, or whether it continued as coparcenary property under Mitakshara law. That distinction can fundamentally alter the rights of the next generation.
 The judgment is particularly relevant in family property disputes where children seek partition of properties standing in their parents’ names. It reinforces that a child’s right by birth is not an automatic right over every asset inherited or held by the father. Equally, it does not give a blanket right to a father to treat every inherited property as his exclusive asset. The legal character of the property, the point at which succession opened and the manner of devolution must be examined before determining whether a claim for partition is maintainable.
